title: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
description: Processes as isolated programs vs threads as workers inside them — memory, context-switch costs, and why sharing memory is both powerful and dangerous.

data.text: **Question:** What is the difference between a process and a thread?

A **process** is a running program with its own isolated memory space — code, heap, and globals are protected from other processes. A **thread** is a unit of execution *inside* a process; all threads of one process share its memory but each has its own stack and instruction pointer. Processes give isolation (one crash doesn't take others down); threads give cheap sharing (but require synchronization to avoid races).

**Process:**
- Own address space, file handles, environment
- Creating one is expensive; switching between processes costs a kernel transition and cache/TLB flushes
- Communication needs explicit mechanisms: pipes, sockets, shared memory, message queues

**Thread:**
- Shares the process's heap and globals; has its own stack and registers
- Creating/switching is much cheaper than processes — but still not free
- Shared memory means race conditions: two threads mutating the same field without locks produce non-deterministic bugs

**In practice:**
- Operating systems schedule *threads* (processes are just containers of threads + resources)
- A modern .NET app: one process, many threads from the thread pool, plus async continuations that may hop threads
- Browsers: each tab is often a separate process now (site isolation) precisely because shared memory between untrusted sites is a security problem
- 'Concurrency vs parallelism': concurrency is structuring work so tasks can interleave; parallelism is executing simultaneously on multiple cores. Threads enable both; a single-threaded async app can be concurrent without being parallel

data.title: Isolation vs shared memory

data.text: Quick recall: isolation vs shared memory, per-thread stack, and why threads need synchronization. Bonus: mention that OS schedules threads, not processes.

items: Saying threads have separate memory — they share the process heap
Claiming threads are free — they carry stack memory and scheduling overhead
Forgetting that async/await doesn't guarantee parallelism
What is a race condition, and how do you prevent one?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Thread: shares its process's memory, cheap-ish, needs synchronization
OS schedules threads; processes are resource containers
data.takeaway: Processes buy isolation, threads buy shared speed — and shared memory is where bugs are born.
